etymology: From Latin multitudo, from multus, many. The Hebrew hāmōn is onomatopoeic in its root sense — it means a murmur, a roar, the noise a great crowd makes — so that the Hebrew for multitude begins with the sound of one and only afterwards means the thing itself. Greek ochlos is the common crowd, the throng, and carries in the Gospels a distinct pathos: the ochlos is the mass of ordinary people, neither the rulers nor the disciples, pressed upon and unshepherded.
biblical_def: A multitude in Scripture is never treated as a moral authority, and the Bible's clearest statement on the subject cuts directly against the instinct of every crowd: “Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment” (Exo 23:2). Numbers do not make a thing right; the command anticipates that they will feel as though they do, and forbids the inference. Yet multitude is not a negative word. In counsel it is a positive good, because many advisers expose what one man cannot see: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — the same book that warns against following the crowd commends consulting many. The Gospels then give the word its most tender use. The Lord Jesus looks at the crowd and does not see a mob or a market: “But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd” (Mat 9:36). And the last vision shows what becomes of the multitudes He came for — not a manageable remnant but a company beyond counting: “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes” (Rev 7:9). Scripture therefore refuses both the flattery of the crowd and the contempt of it.
webster_summary: A great number of persons or things collectively; a crowd or throng; the mass of common people; and in Scripture the crowd Christ pitied as sheep without a shepherd, and the innumerable redeemed multitude before the throne.
webster_full: MULTITUDE, n. 1. The state of being many; a great number, indefinitely.
2. A number collectively; the sum of many; as a multitude of counsellors. Prov. 11.
3. A great number of people assembled; a crowd; a throng.
4. The populace; the mass of men, without reference to rank or condition; the vulgar.
5. In Scripture, thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil. Exod. 23. A great multitude, which no man could number. Rev. 7.
corruption_summary: Majority sentiment is treated as the arbiter of truth and morality, so that a doctrine is judged by how many hold it and a practice justified by how widely it is accepted — the precise reasoning Exodus 23:2 forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic error of a democratic age is to convert a description into a warrant: because most people now think a thing, the thing must be so. The reasoning is invisible because it feels like realism rather than argument, and it operates in the church as readily as outside it, wherever a doctrine is quietly retired on the ground that it has become a minority position. Exo 23:2 was given precisely against this reflex, and it was given first as a rule for courts — do not decline after many to wrest judgment — because the pressure of the crowd on a witness or a judge is the place where the reflex does its most concrete damage. Scripture's counter-examples are relentless: the whole congregation sided with the ten spies against Joshua and Caleb, and the whole multitude cried crucify him. Truth is not settled by counting.

The opposite corruption is an aristocratic contempt for ordinary people, which reads the Gospels' crowds as a fickle mob and concludes that the mass of men are beneath serious spiritual concern. The Lord's own response forbids it. He saw the multitudes and was moved with compassion, and the reason given is a pastoral diagnosis rather than a moral verdict: they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd. Their fickleness was the symptom of having no one to feed them. The principle to recover is that the crowd is neither an authority to be obeyed nor a rabble to be despised, but a field of shepherdless people for whom the appointed remedy is preachers — pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers.
roots_summary: Hebrew hāmōn is a murmur, roar, or tumult, and hence a crowd; rōb is abundance or greatness of number. Greek ochlos is the common throng, and plēthos is a fulness or great number, whence the innumerable multitude of Revelation.
roots_lines: Hebrew hāmōn (H1995) — a noise, murmur, or roar; then the crowd that makes it; then abundance or great number.
Hebrew rōb (H7230) — multitude, abundance, greatness; in the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Pro 11:14).
Greek ochlos (G3793) — a throng or crowd, especially the common people as distinct from rulers; the word used of the multitudes Christ pitied.
Greek plēthos (G4128) — a fulness, great number, multitude; used of the heavenly host (Luk 2:13) and of the whole assembly of believers.
Greek ochlopoieō (G3792) — to gather a crowd, to raise a mob; used of the rabble stirred up against Paul at Thessalonica (Act 17:5).
usage: Of the crowd as no moral warrant: thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil (Exo 23:2).
Of many counsellors as safety: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Pro 11:14).
Of the innumerable redeemed: a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations (Rev 7:9).

etymology: From Old French host, from Latin hostis, originally a stranger and then an enemy, whence hostilis — the army being the stranger-band that comes against you. (The English word for one who entertains guests is a separate line, from Latin hospes.) The Hebrew tsābā' means an organised body mustered for service, whether soldiers, labourers, or the ordered ranks of the stars, and it is the word in the divine title LORD of hosts.
biblical_def: Host is Scripture's word for an ordered array under command, and its range is the measure of God's dominion. It is first used not of armies but of the finished creation: “Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them” (Gen 2:1) — sun, moon, and stars conceived as ranks drawn up, each in its station. From that the divine title follows, and it is the great name of God's sovereignty in the historical books and prophets: “Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Psa 24:10). The hosts are angelic as well as stellar, and the shepherds saw them mustered: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God” (Luk 2:13). Joshua, surveying Jericho, learns that the LORD's host has its own Captain who takes no side but His own: “Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come” (Jos 5:14), and Joshua falls on his face and worships — a thing no created angel accepts. The title becomes a weapon in the mouth of faith when David refuses Goliath's terms and states the real disparity of forces: “Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied” (1Sa 17:45). To confess the LORD of hosts is to say that every ordered power in heaven and earth is already mustered and already commanded.
webster_summary: An army; a great number arrayed for war; the ordered ranks of the heavenly bodies and of the angels; and in the divine title LORD of hosts, the sovereign Commander of every marshalled power in heaven and earth.
webster_full: HOST, n. 1. An army; a number of men embodied for war; a great company.
2. Any great number or multitude; as a host of enemies, a host of friends.
3. The heavenly bodies, conceived as an ordered array; the host of heaven, the sun, moon and stars. Deut. 4.
4. The angels, as the armies of God; the heavenly host. Luke 2.
5. In the title LORD of hosts, Jehovah Sabaoth, the God who commands all the armies of heaven and earth. Psalm 24; 1 Sam. 17.
corruption_summary: The LORD of hosts is treated as an embarrassing relic of tribal warfare to be quietly dropped, and the host of heaven is either mythologised into pagan astral religion or flattened into impersonal natural forces.
corruption_paragraphs: The title LORD of hosts occurs some two hundred and fifty times, and it is among the first casualties when a theology grows uncomfortable with divine power. It is presented as the residue of a warrior deity from Israel's primitive stage, outgrown by the fatherhood revealed in Christ. But the New Testament does not outgrow it; James takes the title untranslated into Greek and turns it against oppressive employers — the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth — and Paul quotes Isaiah's except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed as the ground of the remnant's survival. The title is not a rival to God's fatherhood but its guarantee: a father who cannot command the field cannot protect his children, and the comfort of the name lies exactly in the fact that the forces are His and are already drawn up.

The second corruption concerns the host of heaven. Because Israel's neighbours worshipped the stars, it is argued that Scripture's language of a stellar host is borrowed astral religion imperfectly demythologised. The texts say the reverse with unusual bluntness. The host of heaven is made — finished on the fourth day, ranked with the works of God's fingers — and Deuteronomy explicitly warns Israel against lifting up her eyes and being driven to worship them, because the LORD has divided them unto all nations. Scripture knows exactly what the nations did with the stars and forbids it by name. The principle to recover is that the heavens are an army under orders, not a pantheon and not a machine: they are personal enough to be commanded and impersonal enough that worshipping them is idolatry.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsābā' is an army, a mustered body, or organised service, used of soldiers, of the stars, and of the Levites' ministry; the plural gives Jehovah ts'bā'ōth, LORD of hosts. Greek stratia is an army or band of soldiers.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — army, host, mustered service; used of warriors, of the host of heaven, and of the Levites' appointed service in the tabernacle.
Hebrew Jehovah ts'bā'ōth — the LORD of hosts; the great title of divine sovereignty, taken untranslated into Greek as sabaoth (Jas 5:4; Rom 9:29).
Hebrew ts'bā' hashshāmayim — the host of heaven; the ordered stars (Gen 2:1) and, in the prophets, the angelic court about the throne (1Ki 22:19).
Greek stratia (G4756) — an army, a band of soldiers; the heavenly host of Luk 2:13.
Greek archistratēgos — a chief captain of the host; the Septuagint title of the figure who met Joshua before Jericho (Jos 5:14).
usage: Of the finished creation as an ordered array: the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them (Gen 2:1).
Of the divine title: who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory (Psa 24:10).
Of faith's reckoning of the odds: I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts (1Sa 17:45).

etymology: From Latin tribus, one of the three original divisions of the Roman people. The Hebrew words are more vivid than the English: shebet and matteh both mean a rod, staff, or sceptre, and both came to mean a tribe — the branch that springs from one stock, and the staff that marks a chieftain's authority. When Aaron's rod budded among the twelve rods of the tribes, the pun was the point: the tribe is the rod. Greek phulē is from phuō, to grow or spring up, and carries the same image of a stock branching.
biblical_def: A tribe in Scripture is a household grown into a nation without ceasing to be a household, and the twelve are treated as a fixed and God-given order rather than an accident of descent: “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them; every one according to his blessing he blessed them” (Gen 49:28). The blessings are prophecies, and each tribe's history unfolds along the line Jacob laid down. The tribes are not merely a census category but the shape of worship, going up together to one place: “Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the LORD” (Psa 122:4) — unity without uniformity, twelve distinct companies with one destination and one Name. The whole arrangement narrows at last to a single tribe and a single Person, for the sceptre was promised to Judah and the promise is claimed in heaven: “behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof” (Rev 5:5). And the category is then opened outward rather than abolished, for the redeemed are numbered not as an undifferentiated mass but as a great multitude “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) standing before the throne. Distinction of peoples survives redemption; what does not survive is division and enmity between them.
webster_summary: A family, race, or division of a people descended from one ancestor; specifically one of the twelve divisions of Israel descended from the sons of Jacob; and in Revelation the tribe of Judah from which Christ sprang and the tribes and tongues of the redeemed.
webster_full: TRIBE, n. 1. A family, race, or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor and kept distinct.
2. A division, class, or distinct portion of a people, whether from the same or different ancestors; as the twelve tribes of Israel.
3. In Hebrew, a rod, staff, or sceptre; hence the branch springing from one stock, and the authority borne over it.
4. A number of things having certain characters in common; a class or order.
5. In Scripture, whither the tribes go up. Psalm 122. The Lion of the tribe of Juda. Rev. 5.
corruption_summary: Ethnic and cultural identity is absolutised into the fundamental category of human standing, so that men are classed first by group and judged accordingly — a framework Scripture answers with one-in-Adam and one-in-Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern tribalism that treats group identity as the deepest fact about a person is not the Bible's doctrine of tribes but its inversion. Scripture's anthropology has two universal terms and they are both about standing before God, not standing among men: all are one in Adam, in whom all sinned and die, and the redeemed are one in Christ, in whom there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free. Any framework which makes an inherited group the ground of guilt or of innocence has replaced the categories Scripture actually uses — sin, the fallen heart, covenant faithfulness and covenant breaking — with a category the gospel was given to dissolve. The point is not that ancestry is nothing; it is that ancestry cannot bear the weight of ultimate judgment, and the attempt to make it do so produces the very enmity it claims to cure.

The opposite error is a flattening universalism which supposes that because we are one in Christ, all particular belonging is now suspect — that family, people, and nation are obstacles to be transcended. The last book of the Bible refuses this too. The redeemed multitude is described precisely by nations and kindreds and people and tongues (Rev 7:9); the distinctions are still legible in glory. What is abolished is the wall of partition and the enmity, not the diversity. The principle to recover is that the gospel does not erase the tribes but reconciles them, and that a church which loses either half — the real unity or the real particularity — has ceased to picture what John saw before the throne.
roots_summary: Hebrew shebet and matteh both mean a rod, staff, or sceptre, and by extension a tribe — the branch from one stock under one authority. Greek phulē, from phuō to spring up, is a tribe or clan.
roots_lines: Hebrew shebet (H7626) — rod, staff, sceptre, tribe; the sceptre shall not depart from Judah (Gen 49:10) uses the same word as the tribes themselves.
Hebrew matteh (H4294) — a staff, rod, or branch, and hence a tribe; the twelve rods of Num 17, one for each tribal house, of which Aaron's budded.
Greek phulē (G5443) — a tribe or clan, from phuō, to grow or spring forth; used of the twelve tribes and of the tribes of the earth.
Greek patria (G3965) — a lineage or family descending from a father; rendered kindred in Rev 7:9 and family in Eph 3:15.
Hebrew shebet Yehudah — the tribe of Judah, the royal tribe of the promised sceptre, whence the Lion of the tribe of Juda (Rev 5:5).

Of tribes united in worship: whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD (Psa 122:4).
Of the royal tribe fulfilled in Christ: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda... hath prevailed (Rev 5:5).

etymology: From Latin campus, a field or level plain, whence the field on which an army pitches. The Hebrew machaneh is from chānâh, to encamp or pitch, and means both the act of pitching and the encampment itself. Because Israel spent forty years as a camp rather than a country, the word bears an unusual doctrinal load: the camp was at once a military formation, a city, and a sanctuary precinct, and its ordering was given by God down to the position of each standard.
biblical_def: The camp of Israel was a theological arrangement before it was a military one. Every tribe pitched in an appointed place, and the whole was oriented around one centre: “Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch” (Num 2:2). The tabernacle in the middle meant that the nation slept each night in concentric rings around the presence of God, and that presence made the whole encampment holy ground with practical consequences: “For the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy: that he see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee” (Deu 23:14). Sanitation, sexual purity, and the treatment of the dead were all regulated by that one fact. After the golden calf the arrangement was reversed in judgment, and the meeting-place was put outside: “And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp... And it came to pass, that every one which sought the LORD went out unto the tabernacle” (Exo 33:7). That reversal becomes the pattern of the cross, for Christ suffered outside the gate as the sin offering whose body was burned without the camp, and the summons follows: “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13). The believer's position is settled by where Christ is, and He is outside — which means the safety of the religious establishment is the one place the Christian may not seek.
webster_summary: The ground on which an army pitches its tents; the encampment itself with its ordered ranks; and in Scripture the camp of Israel arrayed about the tabernacle, made holy by God's walking in its midst, and the place outside it where Christ suffered.
webster_full: CAMP, n. 1. The ground on which an army pitch their tents, whether for a night or a longer period.
2. The order or arrangement of tents, or of troops disposed for lodging; the encampment.
3. An army; the whole body of persons encamped; as, the camp of Israel numbered six hundred thousand.
4. In Scripture, the encampment of the Israelites in the wilderness, disposed in ordered ranks about the tabernacle. Num. 2.
5. Without the camp; outside the encampment, the place of the burning of the sin offering, and of the reproach of Christ. Heb. 13.
corruption_summary: The wilderness camp is treated as mere ancient hygiene, so that its holiness legislation is read as primitive taboo rather than as instruction in the nearness of a holy God, and the call to go forth without the camp is domesticated into mild nonconformity.
corruption_paragraphs: The regulations governing the camp — what must be buried, who must be put outside, what renders a man unclean until evening — are commonly explained as an ancient people's sanitary code, given a religious veneer. The text supplies its own reason and it is not hygiene: for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp. The laws exist because God is present, and their purpose is that He see no unclean thing and not turn away. That reading is confirmed by the fact that many of the ordinances have no sanitary value whatever, and by the New Testament's treatment of them as shadows of a moral reality. To reduce them to public health is to miss the lesson the wilderness generation was being taught every day for forty years: that a holy God had moved in next door, and that this is a mercy and a danger at once.

The call of Heb 13:13 suffers a gentler corruption — it is quoted as a general encouragement to be a little countercultural, an endorsement of whatever nonconformity the reader already prefers. Its actual force is exact and costly. The camp in that passage is the whole apparatus of an established religion with divine credentials, temple, priesthood, and altar included; and the writer says Christ was put out of it and died there, so that His people must accept the same expulsion. The mark of the true church is therefore not respectability but a willingness to be located where Christ is, bearing his reproach, since here have we no continuing city. The principle to recover is that the reproach is not incidental to discipleship but is the address at which Christ may be found.
roots_summary: Hebrew machaneh is an encampment or army, from chānâh, to pitch or encamp; the same root gives place-names such as Mahanaim, the two camps. Greek parembolē is a camp, barracks, or army in array.
roots_lines: Hebrew machaneh (H4264) — camp, encampment, army; used of Israel in the wilderness and of the angelic host Jacob met (Gen 32:2).
Hebrew chānâh (H2583) — to pitch a tent, encamp, or lay siege; the angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him (Psa 34:7).
Hebrew Mahanaim — two camps; the place where Jacob, meeting the host of God, named the site for the double encampment of angels and men.
Greek parembolē (G3925) — an encampment, barracks, or army in battle order; used of the castle in Acts and of the camp in Heb 13:11-13.
Greek exō tēs parembolēs — without the camp; the place of the burning of the sin offering and of Christ's suffering outside the gate.
usage: Of the ordered encampment about the tabernacle: every man... by his own standard... about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch (Num 2:2).
Of holiness required by God's presence: the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp... therefore shall thy camp be holy (Deu 23:14).
Of the believer's place with Christ: let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach (Heb 13:13).

etymology: From Old French compaignie, from Late Latin companio, one who eats bread (panis) with (cum) another — a companion is literally a bread-sharer. The etymology is worth keeping, because Scripture's warnings and commendations about company almost always concern the table: with such an one no not to eat, on the one hand; and on the other, the Lord Jesus receiving sinners and eating with them. To keep company is, in the oldest sense of the word, to share a loaf.
biblical_def: Company in Scripture means the persons a man travels, eats, and identifies with, and it is treated as a formative power rather than a neutral circumstance. The word can name a band of heralds, and in one striking verse the company that publishes the good news is a company of women: “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11). It can name the ordinary travelling caravan, and the most sobering use in the Gospels is exactly that — Joseph and Mary lost the Lord Jesus by assuming He was among the familiar crowd: “But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance” (Luk 2:44). It is possible to travel a full day in religious company and not have Christ in it, and the discovery is made only by looking for Him. Against every earthly company the epistle to the Hebrews sets the assembly the believer has already joined: “But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels” (Heb 12:22) — a present tense, not a future one. And the Old Testament's practical wisdom about company runs throughout: he that walketh with wise men shall be wise, but a companion of fools shall be destroyed. What a man consents to belong to, he becomes.
webster_summary: An assembly or band of persons; those with whom one associates or travels; fellowship or companionship itself; and in Scripture the company that published the word, the caravan in which Christ was presumed but absent, and the innumerable company of angels believers have come to.
webster_full: COMPANY, n. 1. Persons assembled together; an assemblage of persons for social or other purposes.
2. An assembly of persons associated for the transaction of business, or for the prosecution of some design.
3. Companionship; fellowship; society; the act of keeping with another. Evil communications corrupt good manners. 1 Cor. 15.
4. A band or body of soldiers; a subdivision of a regiment.
5. In Scripture, great was the company of those that published it. Psalm 68. An innumerable company of angels. Heb. 12.
corruption_summary: The formative power of companionship is denied in the name of authenticity, so that warnings about evil company are dismissed as legalism, while the opposite error withdraws from sinners altogether and calls the withdrawal holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern assumption is that a person's convictions are self-generated and therefore proof against his surroundings — that a man may keep any company he likes and remain what he is. Scripture flatly contradicts it: evil communications corrupt good manners, and a companion of fools shall be destroyed. The apostolic instruction is more specific still, and it concerns the table: Paul commands that with a professing brother who persists in gross sin the church is not to eat, precisely because shared bread signifies shared standing. To call such instruction legalism is to mistake a description of how human beings actually work for an arbitrary rule. Character is caught as much as taught, and the Bible treats the choice of companions as one of the most consequential a young man makes.

The opposite error hears these warnings and withdraws from the world entirely, treating separation from sinners as the substance of holiness. Paul anticipates and forbids the misreading in the same passage: he says he did not mean the fornicators of this world, for then must ye needs go out of the world — the discipline concerns those called a brother, not the unconverted. And the Lord Jesus bore the name of a friend of publicans and sinners without ever contracting their sin. The principle to recover is a double one: the church's table is guarded, and the Christian's life is not. A believer who cannot be found in the company of sinners has misunderstood his commission; a church which cannot say who may sit at the Supper has misunderstood its keys.
roots_summary: Hebrew qāhāl is an assembly or convocation; g'dūd is a troop or raiding band; tsābā' is a mustered host. Greek sunodia is a company travelling the same road, and homilia is association or intercourse, whence the warning of 1Co 15:33.
roots_lines: Hebrew qāhāl (H6951) — assembly, congregation, convocation; the gathered company of Israel before the LORD.
Hebrew g'dūd (H1416) — a band, troop, or raiding party; used of marauders and of David's men.
Greek sunodia (G4923) — a company journeying together, a caravan; the word in Luk 2:44, from sun (with) and hodos (way).
Greek homilia (G3657) — association, companionship, converse; evil communications corrupt good manners (1Co 15:33).
Greek munās / panegyris (G3831) — a festal gathering; paired with the innumerable company of angels in Heb 12:22-23.
usage: Of the heralds of the word: great was the company of those that published it (Psa 68:11).
Of Christ presumed present and absent: supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey (Luk 2:44).
Of the assembly believers have already joined: ye are come... to an innumerable company of angels (Heb 12:22).

etymology: From Old French village, from Latin villa, a country house or farmstead. The Hebrew words distinguish two kinds of settlement: chātsēr is an unwalled place, an enclosure or hamlet lying open, and kāphār is a covered or protected village (whence Capernaum, the village of Nahum). The unwalled character matters legally, for a house in a village without walls could be redeemed at any time under the jubilee statute, being counted with the fields of the country rather than with a walled city.
biblical_def: Villages are where most of the Bible's people actually lived, and Scripture keeps them in view when a merely political history would not. The land settled by Judah after the return is described village by village — “And for the villages, with their fields, some of the children of Judah dwelt at Kirjatharba, and in the villages thereof” (Neh 11:25) — the covenant people rebuilt from the hamlets outward, not from the capital only. The most consequential fact about the villages is that the Lord Jesus went to them. His ministry was not confined to Jerusalem or even to the towns of consequence: “And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people” (Mat 9:35). The unwalled places got the whole gospel and the whole compassion. Even unbelief did not turn Him aside from them but redirected His labour into them: “And he marvelled because of their unbelief. And he went round about the villages, teaching” (Mar 6:6). And the first resurrection appearance at length was granted on a village road, to two men of no rank whatever: “two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was from Jerusalem about threescore furlongs” (Luk 24:13). The risen Christ spent His afternoon opening the Scriptures to a pair of discouraged disciples walking home to a hamlet, which tells us how God apportions His attention.
webster_summary: A small assemblage of houses in the country, less than a town and generally unwalled; in Scripture the open hamlets and their fields, distinguished from walled cities in the law of redemption, and the settlements through which Christ went preaching.
webster_full: VILLAGE, n. 1. A small assemblage of houses, less than a town or city, and inhabited chiefly by farmers and laboring people.
2. In Scripture, an unwalled place or hamlet, with its fields, dependent upon a neighboring city.
3. The houses of the villages which have no wall round about them shall be counted as the fields of the country. Levit. 25.
4. The daughters of a city; the dependent hamlets reckoned with it in the lists of the inheritance. Josh. 15.
5. In Scripture, Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching. Matt. 9. A village called Emmaus. Luke 24.
corruption_summary: Significance is measured by scale and platform, so that small and obscure places are treated as unworthy of serious labour — an assumption the ministry of Christ, conducted largely in villages, contradicts at every point.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is not a redefinition of the word but a settled instinct about worth: that ministry, like everything else, should be measured by reach, and that a labour spent on few people in an unimportant place is a labour wasted. The instinct is not new — Nathanael asked whether any good thing could come out of Nazareth — but modern metrics have given it an appearance of rigour. Scripture's record simply does not support it. The incarnate Son distributed His ministry through cities and villages, gave a whole night's teaching to one man, a whole afternoon to two on the Emmaus road, and His clearest self-disclosure as Messiah to a Samaritan woman at a well. He marvelled at unbelief in one place and answered it by going round about the villages, teaching.

The principle to recover is that God's valuation of a work is not derived from the size of the audience, and that faithfulness in an unwalled place is not a lesser calling awaiting promotion. This bears directly on the pastor of a small congregation, the father teaching a handful of children, and the believer whose whole sphere is a street. Who hath despised the day of small things? is a rebuke, not a lament. The villages of Galilee had the gospel of the kingdom preached in them and every sickness healed among them, and the men who walked to Emmaus heard the risen Christ expound Moses and all the prophets — an exposition the world would give a great deal to recover, delivered on a country road to two people.
roots_summary: Hebrew chātsēr is an enclosure or unwalled village; kāphār is a covered or protected hamlet, giving names like Capernaum. Greek kōmē is a village, and kōmopolis a village-town.
roots_lines: Hebrew chātsēr (H2691) — an enclosure, court, or unwalled village; the same word does duty for the courts of the tabernacle and for open settlements.
Hebrew kāphār (H3723) — a covered or protected village; surviving in Capernaum, K'phar Nachum, the village of Nahum.
Hebrew bānōth — daughters; the idiom by which dependent villages are called the daughters of the city they belong to (Jos 15:45).
Greek kōmē (G2968) — a village or country town; Jesus went about all the cities and villages (Mat 9:35).
Greek kōmopolis (G2969) — a village-town, a place between the two in size; used only in Mar 1:38 of the towns Christ came forth to preach in.
usage: Of the resettled land after the exile: for the villages, with their fields, some of the children of Judah dwelt (Neh 11:25).
Of Christ's itinerant ministry: Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching... and preaching the gospel of the kingdom (Mat 9:35).
Of the road to Emmaus: two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus (Luk 24:13).

etymology: From Latin sub (under, near) and urbs (city) — the ground lying under the walls of a city. The English word has drifted a long way from the Hebrew it renders. Migrāsh is from gārash, to drive out, and means the open land around a town into which the cattle were driven out to pasture. The King James suburbs therefore denotes not a residential district but a common pasture, an inalienable green belt measured out from the wall.
biblical_def: The suburbs of Scripture are the pasture lands granted with the Levitical cities, and they are one of the quiet proofs that God provided for the tribe He gave no inheritance. The Levites received no territorial allotment, because the LORD was their inheritance; instead they received forty-eight cities scattered through every tribe, each with its ring of open ground: “Command the children of Israel, that they give unto the Levites of the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell in; and ye shall give also unto the Levites suburbs for the cities round about them” (Num 35:2). The claim was made at Shiloh on the authority of the word given through Moses, and the purpose is stated plainly — “The LORD commanded by the hand of Moses to give us cities to dwell in, with the suburbs thereof for our cattle” (Jos 21:2). The men who taught Israel the law had to eat, and God did not leave their provision to goodwill. The pasture was also protected in perpetuity against sale: “But the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold; for it is their perpetual possession” (Lev 25:34) — a Levite could fall into debt, but the ground that fed his flock could not be taken from his descendants. Ezekiel's visionary city keeps the same arrangement, measuring out ground about the sanctuary “for the suburbs thereof” (Eze 45:2). The provision is dispersed, secured, and inalienable, and the whole design places teachers of the law within reach of every tribe.
webster_summary: The open pasture ground lying about a city, into which the cattle were driven out; specifically the common lands granted with the forty-eight Levitical cities, which by statute could never be sold.
webster_full: SUBURBS, n. 1. The parts lying without the walls of a city, but adjacent or near to them.
2. In Scripture, the open ground or common pasture about a city, appointed for the cattle. Num. 35.
3. The lands granted with the cities of the Levites, measured a thousand cubits round about from the wall.
4. That which is inalienable; the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold, for it is their perpetual possession. Levit. 25.
5. In the Hebrew, from a root signifying to drive out; the place whither the herds were driven forth to feed.
corruption_summary: Provision for those who teach the word is treated as an embarrassment or a mark of mercenary religion, though Scripture makes it a divine command; and at the other extreme the principle is stretched to justify accumulation far beyond a pasture and a house.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live issue is the doctrine the suburbs embody: that God commands material provision for those set apart to teach His word. Modern suspicion of paid ministry — the assumption that a man who receives support has a motive to flatter — treats such provision as a concession at best. Scripture treats it as an ordinance, and the New Testament argues from precisely these Levitical arrangements: do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel. The Levite's pasture was not a salary negotiated with the congregation; it was measured out by divine command and made unsellable, so that no generation could vote its teachers into poverty.

The opposite abuse is real and the same passage rebukes it. The Levite was given a city to dwell in and ground for his cattle — sufficiency, not estate. He received no tribal inheritance at all, and the reason given is that the LORD was his inheritance; the arrangement was designed to keep him dependent and dispersed rather than landed and concentrated. When ministers of religion have accumulated territory and revenue beyond that measure, the result in every century has been the corruption of the office. The principle to recover holds both ends: a congregation that starves its teachers is disobeying a command, and a ministry that enriches itself has forgotten that its portion was always meant to be the LORD Himself, with a field for the cattle.
roots_summary: Hebrew migrāsh is common land or pasture about a city, from gārash, to drive out — the ground into which the herds were driven. It occurs chiefly in Numbers 35, Joshua 21, Chronicles, and Ezekiel's visionary allotment.
roots_lines: Hebrew migrāsh (H4054) — common land, open pasture, suburb; the ring of ground measured out about each Levitical city.
Hebrew gārash (H1644) — to drive out, expel, cast forth; the root sense is the driving out of the cattle to feed.
Hebrew 'alpāyim 'ammâh — two thousand cubits; the measure of the suburbs on each side of the city in Num 35:5.
Hebrew nachalâh (H5159) — inheritance; the word denied to Levi, of whom it is said the LORD is his inheritance (Deu 18:2).
Levitical cities — forty-eight in all, including the six cities of refuge, dispersed through every tribe so that no region lacked teachers of the law.
usage: Of the grant to the Levites: give also unto the Levites suburbs for the cities round about them (Num 35:2).
Of the claim made at Shiloh: cities to dwell in, with the suburbs thereof for our cattle (Jos 21:2).
Of the inalienable pasture: the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold; for it is their perpetual possession (Lev 25:34).

Command the children of Israel, that they give unto the Levites of the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell in; and ye shall give also unto the Levites suburbs for the cities round about them.
Joshua 21:2
And they spake unto them at Shiloh in the land of Canaan, saying, The LORD commanded by the hand of Moses to give us cities to dwell in, with the suburbs thereof for our cattle.
Leviticus 25:34
But the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold; for it is their perpetual possession.
Ezekiel 45:2
Of this there shall be for the sanctuary five hundred in length, with five hundred in breadth, square round about; and fifty cubits round about for the suburbs thereof.

etymology: From Old English wīfman, a compound of wīf (woman, wife) and man (human being) — so that the English word preserves, by accident, the very structure of Gen 2:23. The Hebrew does it deliberately and audibly: the man is 'īsh and the woman is 'ishshâh, and Adam's naming is a pun no translation can carry — she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. The name is itself a doctrine of origin, distinction, and correspondence.
biblical_def: Woman is a creational category, given by God, embodied, and not self-assigned. She is made last and made deliberately, not from the ground as the man was but from the man himself, so that her origin declares both her equality of nature and her distinctness of person: “And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man” (Gen 2:22). She bears the image of God fully and equally — male and female created he them — and she is given an order within that equality, for the man was not created for the woman, but the woman for the man. The fall came through her deception, which Scripture records without excusing the man, who was not deceived and yet ate: “And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression” (1Ti 2:14). Yet the first promise of the gospel is spoken to her adversary about her offspring: “I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel” (Gen 3:15). The whole redemptive line runs through the seed of the woman, and it terminates in an event described in exactly those terms: “God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal 4:4). The dignity Scripture assigns to woman is therefore not honorary. It is a share in the image, a distinct calling, and the instrument through which the Redeemer entered the world. And her praise is located where the world never looks for it: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Pro 31:30).
webster_summary: The female of the human race, made by God from the man and for the man, equally an image-bearer with him; and in Scripture the one through whose seed the Redeemer was promised and of whom the Son of God was made.
webster_full: WOMAN, n. 1. The female of the human race, grown to adult years.
2. A female attendant or servant; also, the sex taken collectively; as, woman is the glory of the man. 1 Cor. 11.
3. In the Hebrew, ishshah, so called from ish, man, because she was taken out of man. Gen. 2.
4. A wife; as, the woman of a household. Every man shall have his own wife. 1 Cor. 7.
5. In Scripture, the seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head. Gen. 3. Made of a woman, made under the law. Gal. 4.
corruption_summary: Womanhood is severed from the body and redefined as an inward identity anyone may claim, so that the creational category of Genesis 1:27 is emptied; and in the opposite direction, the woman's equal bearing of the divine image is denied in practice by contempt or domination.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing modern corruption is the claim that woman names an inward sense of identity rather than an embodied creational reality — that the category is assigned rather than given, and can therefore be adopted, exited, or held by anyone who declares it. Scripture's account is unambiguous and it is an account of bodies: God made them male and female, made the woman from the man's side, and the Lord Jesus grounds His teaching on marriage in the fact that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female. This is not a cultural convention that Genesis happens to report; it is presented as the act of the Creator, and it is the premise of the marriage covenant, of the promise of the woman's seed, and of the incarnation itself, in which the Son was made of a woman. A category which can be claimed at will cannot bear any of that weight. The dictionary affirms the image of God in every person who suffers under this confusion, and refuses the framework precisely because the framework cannot give them what they were made for.

The opposite corruption is older and has done its own great damage: the denial in practice of the woman's equal standing before God. Where Scripture says male and female created he them, in the image of God, some have inferred from the order of creation a difference of worth, and treated headship as licence for contempt, domination, or neglect. The apostles forbid the inference explicitly. Husbands are commanded to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it, to dwell with them according to knowledge, and to honour them as heirs together of the grace of life — with the striking sanction that failure here obstructs a man's prayers. The principle to recover holds both truths at once: equal in nature, dignity, and inheritance; distinct in creation, calling, and order. Scripture never trades one for the other, and every corruption of this doctrine is an attempt to be rid of one half.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ishshâh is woman or wife, formed from 'īsh, man, and preserving the pun of Gen 2:23. Greek gunē means woman or wife according to context, and thēlus is the female as a creational category in Gen 1:27 and Mat 19:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ishshâh (H802) — woman, wife, female; named from 'īsh, man, because she was taken out of man (Gen 2:23).
Hebrew n'qēbâh (H5347) — female, the creational counterpart to zākār, male; male and female created he them (Gen 1:27).
Hebrew 'ēzer k'negdō — a help meet for him, literally a helper corresponding to him; 'ēzer is elsewhere used of God Himself as Israel's help.
Greek gunē (G1135) — woman or wife; made of a woman, made under the law (Gal 4:4).
Greek thēlus (G2338) — female; used by Christ in Mat 19:4 quoting Genesis, and by Paul in Gal 3:28 of standing in Christ.
usage: Of her creation and correspondence: the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman (Gen 2:22).
Of the promise through her seed: I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed (Gen 3:15).
Of the praise Scripture assigns her: a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised (Pro 31:30).

pos: adj. and n. (rendering Hebrew rō'sh, Greek prōtos and archē in compounds)
etymology: From Old French chief, from Latin caput, the head. The Hebrew rō'sh likewise means head and then, by the same natural extension, first, foremost, or principal. Greek forms the idea by compounding archē — whence archiereus, chief priest; architektōn, master builder; and, in a phrase found nowhere in Greek literature before Peter used it, archipoimēn, chief Shepherd.
biblical_def: Chief in Scripture is a word about rank, and the New Testament takes hold of it in order to turn it inside out. The Lord Jesus does not deny that there is a chief place; He redefines the road to it: “And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant” (Mat 20:27). The ambition is not forbidden but redirected, and the redirection is total, since the way up is the way down and the currency of greatness is service. Paul then applies the word to himself in the one category no man competes for: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1Ti 1:15) — written not in his unconverted days but as an apostle, in the present tense, so that the chiefest of the apostles reckons himself chiefest of sinners and finds the two entirely compatible. The word marks out Christ Himself in two great titles. He is the foundation stone that governs the whole structure: “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20); and He is the Shepherd over every under-shepherd, whose appearing is the day of reckoning and reward: “And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away” (1Pe 5:4). Chief is finally used of what a man loves most, and the psalmist in exile makes his own affections the test: if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth. Every man has a chief joy; the question is only what it is.
webster_summary: Highest in rank, office, or importance; first or principal; and as a noun the head or leader of a body of men — whence chief priest, chief corner stone, chief Shepherd, and Paul's confession that he is chief of sinners.
webster_full: CHIEF, adj. 1. Highest in office or rank; principal; as a chief priest, the chief butler.
2. Principal or most eminent in any quality or action; most distinguished; as the chief excellence of a work.
3. First in affection, or in the estimation of the mind; as, my chief joy. Psalm 137.
4. n. A commander; a leader; the person highest in authority over a body of men.
5. In Scripture, whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant. Matt. 20. The chief corner stone. Eph. 2. The chief Shepherd. 1 Pet. 5.
corruption_summary: Servant language is annexed to leadership without altering it, so that the vocabulary of Matthew 20 decorates the same hierarchies of ambition and status it was given to overturn.
corruption_paragraphs: The command of Mat 20:27 has been so thoroughly absorbed into the language of modern leadership that it can now be quoted without cost. Servant terminology is applied to offices whose actual operation — the pursuit of platform, the guarding of position, the assessment of people by their usefulness — is untouched by it. The Lord's words were not a style of leading but a reversal of the thing itself: the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them; but it shall not be so among you. The mark of the reversal is concrete and unmistakable, since it appears where advantage is surrendered rather than where humility is expressed. He who washed feet and went to a cross set the standard, and He set it in actions no vocabulary can imitate.

The corruption has a mirror image in which the word chief is thought to be abolished altogether — as though Christ had taught that there is no rank, no office, and no authority in the church. He taught nothing of the kind. He appointed apostles, the New Testament names elders who rule and are worthy of double honour, and Peter, writing to elders, warns them against lording it over God's heritage while assuming they genuinely oversee the flock. Authority is real and is answerable, which is exactly why the chief Shepherd's appearing is set before them as both incentive and reckoning (1Pe 5:4). The principle to recover is that Scripture abolishes neither office nor ambition but reassigns them: office exists for the flock's good, and the only ambition it permits is to be spent.
roots_summary: Hebrew rō'sh is head, top, or chief, whence first and principal. Greek expresses the idea by prōtos, first, and by compounds of archē — archiereus (chief priest), archipoimēn (chief Shepherd), akrogōniaios (chief corner stone).
roots_lines: Hebrew rō'sh (H7218) — head, top, chief, beginning; the head of a house, the top of a mountain, and the first of a series alike.
Greek prōtos (G4413) — first, foremost, chief; of whom I am chief (1Ti 1:15) and whosoever will be chief among you (Mat 20:27).
Greek archipoimēn (G750) — chief Shepherd; a compound found only at 1Pe 5:4, setting Christ over every under-shepherd.
Greek akrogōniaios (G204) — chief corner stone, the stone at the extreme angle governing the alignment of two walls (Eph 2:20).
Greek archiereus (G749) — chief priest or high priest; used both of the Aaronic office and, in Hebrews, of Christ's greater priesthood.
usage: Of the way to greatness: whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant (Mat 20:27).
Of Paul's estimate of himself: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief (1Ti 1:15).
Of Christ's titles: the chief corner stone (Eph 2:20); the chief Shepherd shall appear (1Pe 5:4).

And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant:
1 Timothy 1:15
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
Ephesians 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
1 Peter 5:4
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.

etymology: From Old English geoguth, cognate with young. The Hebrew n''ūrīm is a plural form — literally young-times, the years of one's youth taken together as a season rather than an age — and it covers everything from childhood to full manhood before marriage and establishment. It is the season Scripture treats as decisive, because habits, loyalties, and the fear of God are all set in it.
biblical_def: Youth in Scripture is a season of strength, of peculiar danger, and above all of opportunity that does not return. The great charge is Solomon's, and it is urgent because of what follows it: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them” (Ecc 12:1). The argument is not that old age cannot repent but that it is a poor season to begin, when strength is spent and appetite for God has grown cold along with every other appetite. Where youth is given to God, it establishes a lifetime of confidence: “For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth” (Psa 71:5) — the psalm of an old man looking back on an early trust that carried him. Jeremiah puts the same relation in the tenderest terms, calling God the guide of one's youth: “Wilt thou not from this time cry unto me, My father, thou art the guide of my youth?” (Jer 3:4). Youth is not therefore a period of exemption from serious service; Paul tells a young minister to refuse that excuse and to answer contempt with conduct: “Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity” (1Ti 4:12). The way to be taken seriously young is not to demand it but to be exemplary. And for the aged there is a promise that reverses the natural direction of things: God satisfieth thy mouth with good things, so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle's (Psa 103:5).
webster_summary: The early part of life, from childhood to full manhood; the state of being young; and in Scripture the season in which the Creator is to be remembered, in which flight from lust is commanded, and which God renews in those who trust Him.
webster_full: YOUTH, n. 1. The part of life that succeeds to childhood; the period from childhood to manhood.
2. A young man; the state of being young; as, in the vigor of youth.
3. Young persons collectively; as, the youth of a nation.
4. The first or early part of any thing; as, the youth of the year. Flee also youthful lusts. 2 Tim. 2.
5. In Scripture, remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth. Eccl. 12. Let no man despise thy youth. 1 Tim. 4.
corruption_summary: Youth is redefined as a protected season of experimentation in which commitment is premature and moral seriousness is unhealthy, so that the years Scripture calls decisive are spent precisely as Ecclesiastes warns against.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of youth — extended for a decade beyond anything previous generations knew — treats the young years as a moratorium: a time to postpone commitment, sample identities, and defer the fear of God until the serious part of life begins. Ecc 12:1 addresses that exact proposal and reverses it. Remember now is set against while the evil days come not, and the whole passage that follows is a portrait of faculties failing one by one — the keepers of the house trembling, those that look out of the windows darkened — so that the man who postponed God arrives at Him with nothing left to bring. Scripture's charge is not that the young should be joyless; the same book says rejoice, O young man, in thy youth. It is that they should rejoice knowing that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment, which is a very different thing from a moratorium.

The corresponding error in the church is to treat the young as incapable of anything but being entertained until they are old enough to matter — the assumption behind a great deal of youth ministry, and the one Paul forbids Timothy to accept. Let no man despise thy youth is not a demand for deference; the remedy prescribed is that Timothy be an example to the believers in word, conversation, charity, spirit, faith, and purity. Scripture's record is full of young people carrying real weight: Joseph, David, Josiah crowned at eight and seeking God at sixteen, Daniel and his companions, Mary. The principle to recover is that youth is a season of strength to be spent rather than a waiting room, and that a church which asks little of its young people should not be surprised when they conclude that little is at stake.
roots_summary: Hebrew n''ūrīm is the plural noun for the time of youth, from na'ar, a boy or young man; bachūr is a chosen young man in his prime. Greek neotēs is youth, from neos, new or young.
roots_lines: Hebrew n''ūrīm (H5271) — the days of youth, taken as a season; the wife of thy youth (Mal 2:14) and the guide of my youth (Jer 3:4).
Hebrew na'ar (H5288) — a boy, lad, or young man; used of Samuel serving in the tabernacle and of David before Goliath.
Hebrew bachūr (H970) — a young man in his prime, literally one chosen or tested; the glory of young men is their strength (Pro 20:29).
Greek neotēs (G3503) — youth, the state of being young; let no man despise thy youth (1Ti 4:12).
Greek neōterikos (G3512) — youthful, belonging to youth; flee also youthful lusts (2Ti 2:22), where the remedy is flight and not management.
usage: Of the charge to remember early: remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth (Ecc 12:1).
Of a lifelong trust begun young: thou art my trust from my youth (Psa 71:5).
Of youth answering contempt with example: let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers (1Ti 4:12).
